title: Search indexes
tagline: An inverted index turns "which documents contain these words" into a lookup, and BM25 decides which come first.
why:
A SQL WHERE title LIKE '%clinic%' cannot use a normal B-tree index, so it scans every row. It also cannot rank: it does not know that a short clinic name containing "vaccination" is a better match than a long page that mentions it once, or that "clinics" should match "clinic".

A search engine solves both. It builds an inverted index at write time, so a query becomes a few dictionary lookups and a merge, and it scores matches by relevance. OpenSearch and Elasticsearch (both built on Lucene) are the usual answer in an interview.

The index is a derived copy of data that lives in your main database. The design question is as much about keeping that copy in sync as about the search itself.
how:
Tokenising (analysis). At index time each text field goes through an analyzer: split into tokens, lowercase, drop or keep stop words, and often stem ("clinics" → "clinic"). The same analyzer runs on the query, so both sides match. For prefix search ("vacc" → vaccination) index edge n-grams or use a completion suggester.

Inverted index. For every term, a sorted postings list of the documents that contain it, with term frequency and positions. A query for polyclinic bedok fetches two postings lists and intersects or unions them. Positions make phrase queries possible.

Ranking with BM25. The default scoring in Lucene. Three ideas:

  • IDF: rare terms count more. "Bedok" is more informative than "the".
  • Term frequency with saturation: more occurrences help, but the tenth adds little (parameter k1, default 1.2).
  • Length normalisation: a match in a short field beats the same match in a long one (parameter b, default 0.75).

Combine the text score with filters (status, region) and business signals (recency, popularity) in the query.

OpenSearch layout. An index is split into primary shards (Lucene indexes) spread across nodes, each with replicas for availability and read throughput. A query fans out to every shard and the coordinating node merges the top results. New documents become searchable after a refresh, every 1 s by default: search is near real time, not immediate.

Keeping it in sync. Do not dual-write from the app (one write can fail and the copies drift). Use change data capture: read the database's change log (for example Debezium on the Postgres WAL), publish events to Kafka, and have an indexer bulk-upsert documents. Use the row's version or log position so an older event never overwrites a newer one. For mapping changes, build a new index in the background and swap an alias.

steps.note: An admin renames clinic 7. The write goes to the normal service, which knows nothing about search.
The database commits the change. It is the source of truth; the index is a copy you can always rebuild.
The CDC connector reads the committed change from the write-ahead log, so it never sees a change that rolled back and never misses one the app forgot to publish.
An event with the row and its log position lands on a Kafka topic, partitioned by clinic id so changes to one clinic stay in order.
The indexer sends the document in a _bulk request; OpenSearch runs the analyzer when it indexes it. The log position goes in as an external version, so an older event cannot overwrite a newer one.
The document becomes searchable after the next refresh, 1 s by default. End to end, expect a lag of about 1 to 5 s.
The user types polyclinic bedok. The API adds filters the user cannot change, such as status = open.
A bool query: a match on name and address scored by BM25, plus filters, which are cached and do not affect the score.
The query runs on every shard in parallel. Each looks up the postings lists for polyclinic and bedok and returns its top hits; the coordinating node merges them.
The top 20 ids, scores and stored fields come back, typically in tens of milliseconds.
Results are near real time. If a detail must be exact (stock, slots left), read it from the database for the 20 results shown.

tradeoffs.pro: No extra system, transactional, always in sync. Enough for millions of rows and simple ranking.
tradeoffs.con: Less control over analyzers and relevance, and search load competes with the primary workload.

tradeoffs.pro: Rich analyzers, BM25 ranking, facets, fuzzy matching and horizontal scaling by shards.
tradeoffs.con: Another cluster to run, eventual consistency, and a sync pipeline to build and monitor.
Partial failures leave the index permanently out of sync, and writes from other paths are missed.

tradeoffs.pro: Every committed change reaches the index, in order per row, from one place.
tradeoffs.con: More moving parts (connector, Kafka, indexer) and a few seconds of lag.

numbers: OpenSearch refresh interval: 1 s by default, so new documents are searchable after about a second. Raise it during bulk loads.
Common shard sizing guidance: 10 to 50 GB per shard. 200 GB of documents at 25 to 50 GB each ≈ 4 to 8 primary shards, each with 1 replica.
Bulk indexing: batches of about 5 to 15 MB per _bulk request are a common starting point.
Deep paging limit: from + size is capped at 10,000 hits by default; use search_after to go further.
say: The database stays the source of truth; search is a derived index that I keep in sync with change data capture, so I never dual-write.
Text fields go through an analyzer that lowercases and stems, the same analyzer runs on the query, and BM25 ranks rare terms and short fields higher.
Search results are near real time, about a second behind, so anything that must be exact, like slots left, I re-read from the database for the results on screen.
pitfalls: Using the search index as the source of truth. It can be dropped and rebuilt; the database cannot.
Dual writes from the app to the database and the index. One fails, and nothing ever repairs the difference.
Ignoring ordering in the sync pipeline. Two quick updates processed out of order leave the older one in the index. Use versions.
Changing a field's analyzer in place. Existing documents keep the old tokens; build a new index and swap an alias.
Too many tiny shards, or one huge one. Each shard has fixed overhead, and the primary shard count is fixed when the index is created: changing it needs the split or shrink API, or a reindex.

quiz.q: What does an inverted index map?
options: Each term to the list of documents (and positions) that contain it
Each user to their recent queries
quiz.why: Term → postings list. A query looks up the postings lists for its terms and merges them, instead of scanning every document.

quiz.q: Under BM25, which document likely scores higher for bedok?
options: A 2,000-word page that mentions Bedok once
quiz.why: Length normalisation (b) boosts a match in a short field. The same term in a long document counts for less.

quiz.q: A clinic is renamed in Postgres but search still shows the old name an hour later. The app writes to both stores. What is the robust fix?
options: Lower the refresh interval to 100 ms
Sync the index from the database's change log (CDC) with versioned upserts
quiz.why: Dual writes drift when one write fails. CDC sends every committed change, in order, and versions stop older events from winning.

quiz.q: Why can a just-indexed document be missing from results for a moment?
options: It becomes searchable only after the next refresh (1 s by default)
Replicas are always a day behind
quiz.why: OpenSearch is near real time: new segments are opened for search on refresh. Plan for about a second of lag, more through a CDC pipeline.
